name: Tomas Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI firms, employers, unions, parties and government; we don't sell anything or campaign. Your answers are confidential, so please give me the line you'd say outside and the thought you'd keep to yourself. What happens on an ordinary day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage five planners at a large food distributor. Before sunrise we decide which depots get the short deliveries of milk and frozen goods, then I call store managers when their order must change. I use AI every day to compare routes and draft the first allocation list, but drivers phone me when a road closes and I have to make the final call.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is satisfying, and what follows you home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: When a late truck still gets the children's meals to the right stores, I feel I've earned the day. I have a bachelor's degree and enough experience to run a shift, though I'm no genius at it; the drivers often know a better route. I'm 27, single and renting alone. The night allowance gives me pay above many managers nearby, and I've saved about nine months of expenses because my aunt taught me not to spend a good season twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The route tool already saves me a little time, so a ceiling on it would be fine. Stores still need a person to hear that twelve crates are missing, and I know those calls. Diesel prices and night staffing bother me more than a modest bit of software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the drivers the computer can suggest a route, but their road reports still matter. I'd tell friends the tool is useful for the first list, not magic. I would keep showing up for the night shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd keep my job and my good allowance. There are plenty of other depots nearby if this firm ever cuts a shift, and nine months of expenses gives me room to choose. The harder part is finding enough people willing to work nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this week I'd keep the five planners on the same rota and check the route tool's suggested loads with the drivers before dispatch. Through the first year of a plateau I'd stay in this post and add 200 a month from my night allowance to my emergency account. I would keep visiting my aunt on Sundays; I don't need a technology story to change that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my pay. Tired from the hours, but that was true yesterday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would a driver change your morning plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Tuesday our driver Jamil knew the bridge was closed before the map updated. We sent the milk through the market road and lost forty minutes, not half a day. A screen doesn't smell a traffic jam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your aunt say about that extra saving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She asks whether I still buy lunch from the depot café every shift. I do, and she rolls her eyes. I can save the 200 without pretending I'm going to live on bread and water.

say: I'd tell drivers their **road reports** shape each route before dispatch.
I'd tell friends the AI list saves time but doesn't replace **store calls** about missing crates.
think: My **pay and shift** feel safe if AI stays a modest tool.
Nine months saved and **nearby depots** give me other choices if staffing changes.
do: Check **suggested loads** with drivers before dispatch each night.
Add **200 monthly** from the night allowance to emergency savings.
feel: I feel **calm** about my pay, though night work leaves me tired.
S0.quote: A screen doesn't smell a traffic jam.
fieldNote: He uses AI for **first drafts**, while drivers and store calls still shape his final decision.
His **nine-month reserve** and night allowance make ordinary uncertainty manageable.
He wants to keep **Sunday visits** with his aunt, whose saving advice he follows.

steps.text: Check AI load suggestions with drivers before dispatching each night
Add 200 monthly from the night allowance to emergency savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning and buying are exactly the tasks in our office. A stronger system could make the allocation list, answer stores and book lorries, while the warehouse staff still load crates by hand. My five planners could become two, and I don't know whether I'd be one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we should test the route and shortage decisions on actual late-delivery days, not a tidy demonstration. To friends I'd say firms have to compete, and people need a fair chance to learn the new work. I wouldn't tell the team their posts are safe when I haven't seen a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI every shift, yet that doesn't make me the best manager in the building. If two planners can cover what five do now, the company may keep the other shift lead instead of me. The savings protect my rent for a while, but I still want a wage and a trade I can do well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In December I'd ask to run a six-week trial using past shortage days, with the drivers checking what the tool would have sent. I'd learn its dispatch controls myself and, if the director approves, put only routine store replies through it while a planner handles missing food for schools. During the first year of rollout I'd save another 300 a month from the allowance and ask about posted depot operations jobs, without leaving my paid shift for a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turns into anxious when I picture two chairs instead of five. I'm not broke, but I don't like the odds being chosen in a meeting I never attend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep a person on school deliveries?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A school kitchen cannot serve a forecast. If a lorry misses a pallet, a planner has to call the cook and find another depot with actual food. I would test the software there too, but I wouldn't quietly let it send an apology instead of lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your planners about a possible cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd share the trial results and ask the director for the staffing number in writing. I owe them that much, even if I think the market will move on. My aunt would call it keeping my word.

say: I'd test the tool on **late deliveries**, with drivers checking its proposed decisions.
I'd tell the team they deserve a **written headcount plan**, even when firms must compete.
think: My **own shift lead post** could disappear when five planners become two.
Savings cover rent for a while, but I still need **paid work**.
do: Run a **six-week past-case trial** if the director approves.
Learn the **dispatch controls** and automate only routine store replies.
Save **300 monthly** and check posted depot operations jobs.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my own seat and the planners' seats.
S1.quote: A school kitchen cannot serve a forecast.
fieldNote: He supports **competition and training** but will not promise jobs before seeing a written number.
His **average skill** matters to him; daily AI use does not guarantee he survives a smaller team.
The **school delivery example** defines the kind of customer call he would keep with a person.

steps.text: Learn the dispatch controls during a six-week approved trial
Automate routine store replies only if the director approves
Save 300 monthly from the night allowance during rollout
Check posted depot operations jobs while keeping the paid shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it can do almost every thinking task by 2028, our route decisions, exception calls and my supervision are exposed then. The warehouse still has people lifting and checking chilled crates until robots around 2031, but I don't get to call my desk a lifting job. I might lose the allowance and the salary together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team the date on the card and ask for a written notice period. I'd tell my aunt I can pay my rent for months, but I need to look beyond planning. Publicly I'd say a firm should train people for real openings, not promise that every old role survives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could be cut in 2028 even if I help bring the system in. Losing the high night wage would sting, but nine months of expenses and several nearby depots let me search without missing rent straight away. My aunt could offer a spare room if I really needed it, though I don't plan around her pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this month I'd keep my nine-month cash reserve intact and ask the cold-store manager for a paid two-day trial handling temperature checks and damaged crates. I'd take the trial only if my own shift is covered and safety training is provided. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my desk post ends, I'd apply for a posted floor supervisor vacancy only if its wage covers rent; if there is none, I'd use the reserve for a search across the nearby depots while physical warehouse work still needs hands until around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not without a floor under me. The short clock makes the choice narrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a floor supervisor escape the thinking system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, its rotas and stock reports could change in 2028 too. I'd need the role to include real temperature and damage checks, and I don't know if the company would keep enough supervisors for that. The hands-on part lasts longer in this picture, not the title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a paid trial rather than paying for a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can afford a course, but I want to see the work before I spend on it. My aunt's advice is to earn while learning if a company needs the skill. A certificate without a vacancy doesn't put food in my fridge.

say: I'd ask for **written notice** and training tied to real openings.
I'd tell my aunt my **planning desk** could go before robots change the warehouse floor.
think: I could lose the **night wage and post** in 2028.
Nine months saved and **several nearby depots** let me search without missing rent immediately.
do: Request a **paid two-day cold-store trial** with safety training and shift cover.
Apply after 2028 for a **posted floor role** only if its pay covers rent.
Use the **cash reserve** for a nearby-depot search if no floor role opens.
feel: I feel **anxious** under the short clock, though cash and local choices help.
S2.quote: A certificate without a vacancy doesn't put food in my fridge.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **2028 desk exposure** from physical checks before robots arrive around 2031.
His **nine-month reserve** and many nearby depots soften, but do not erase, salary risk.
A floor move depends on **paid training** and affordable wages, not a guaranteed opening.

steps.text: Complete a paid cold-store trial if shift cover and safety training are provided
Apply for a posted floor supervisor job after 2028 only if pay covers rent
Search nearby depots using savings if no floor vacancy opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to learn the cold chain, meaning how food stays at a safe temperature from depot to store. My planning office still faces AGI in 2031, and robots reach the physical floor around 2034. I could move before the desk changes, but I need an actual paid floor opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team we have years to get a qualification while earning, if the company offers one. I'd say at home that I want work I can point to, not just a smarter route screen. I would not claim depot floor jobs are permanent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could earn less but stay employed if I move into checking temperature and loads. The drop is manageable with nine months saved, but I won't assume a floor supervisor survives when its rota and reports can be automated in 2031. I'd rather test the work now than take a title on trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I'd apply for the distributor's paid cold-chain training place if one is funded, and complete the supervised shifts only if they fit my schedule. I'd keep saving 200 a month while my night allowance continues. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd take a posted depot quality role only if its wage covers rent and it includes real physical checks; if it doesn't, I'd search the other distributors rather than spend the reserve on a blind course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried about whether a lower wage would cover groceries. Five years lets me practise instead of guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check on the floor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd record a crate's temperature at the door, open damaged boxes with the trained worker and trace the shipment number. A spreadsheet can tell me where a crate should be; I need to see where it actually is. I'd be a beginner at those checks, and the old hands would know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept a lower wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it pays rent and leaves enough for groceries, yes. I can draw on savings during the training, but I won't spend nine months of cash just to hold a supervisor title. My aunt would ask what the title actually pays.

Save **200 monthly** while the night allowance continues.
Take a **posted quality role** after 2031 only if pay covers rent and groceries and physical checks remain.
feel: I feel **anxious** about lower pay and uncertain openings, despite time to practise.

Save 200 monthly while night allowance continues

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long working stretch at 27. I could keep the good night wage, build a cushion and learn the depot floor in stages before thinking AGI arrives in 2036. Robots doing hands-on checks around 2039 would still change that work, so I wouldn't mortgage my future on one depot skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger planners to learn their craft and take paid training when a company offers it. I'd say firms should invest in people who turn up and do the job, and family can help when someone has to start again. I wouldn't tell people a decade of notice makes every worker equally rich.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could save enough to buy a small home without borrowing everything and still have emergency cash. A planning title won't carry me past 2036, but experience across desk and floor might keep me employed at a depot. There are many nearby firms, although their systems could change together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2027 I'd ask the operations director for one paid floor shift a month, and if approved I'd work those shifts with a trained checker. I'd set aside 400 a month from the night allowance toward a home deposit only after keeping nine months of expenses untouched. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd apply for a posted depot quality opening if it has paid physical duties and covers rent; otherwise I'd stay on notice and search the nearby firms with my cash buffer, knowing robots may change floor work around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. I can use ten years without pretending I know exactly what each depot will buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep nine months aside if you want a home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A deposit is not a meal or rent when wages stop. My aunt took me to the bank when I got my first proper pay and made me open two accounts. I still keep house money separate from emergency money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a home before knowing what robots do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only a place I could afford on a lower wage, and I would keep the emergency account after the purchase. I won't buy just because a bank offers a bigger loan. A house should make life steadier, not trap me in the wrong job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is hardest. Two years could take the allocation calls before I find out whether I can do the physical depot role I'm considering. A paid trial on the cold-store floor, clear notice from the distributor and a real vacancy at a wage I can live on would help. I have savings, but I don't want to spend them chasing a job that was never there.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens at four in the morning when a delivery fails and the school kitchens are waiting. The software can send a new route, but a store manager still needs someone to explain the missing crates. I would rather own a mistake than hide it behind a screen.

headlineQuote: I would rather own a mistake than hide it behind a screen.
portrait: Tomas, **27**, runs a five-person food allocation shift at a large distributor and uses AI daily for routes and draft orders.
His **bachelor's degree** and ordinary skill sit beside practical experience; night pay is high, and he has nine months saved.
He is **single and rents alone**, with many nearby depots and an aunt whose saving advice he follows.
Fast AGI threatens his **desk allocation calls**; with time, he would test paid cold-store work while weighing its later robot risk.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his allocation work before he tests a real depot vacancy.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid floor trial** and a real cold-store opening with a wage that covers his rent.
**Clear notice** before his distributor cuts desk roles, so he can search while still paid.
